claims.claim: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter typical for LC axons.
claims.source: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) typical for LC axons (Reimer et al., 2016), rapid responses to air puffs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) as previously reported (Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019), and increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decayed during the locomotion bout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) consistent with earlier work (Reimer et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: LC axons show rapid responses to air puffs.
claims.source: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) typical for LC axons (Reimer et al., 2016), rapid responses to air puffs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) as previously reported (Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019), and increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decayed during the locomotion bout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) consistent with earlier work (Reimer et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: LC axons show increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decay during the locomotion bout.
claims.source: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) typical for LC axons (Reimer et al., 2016), rapid responses to air puffs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) as previously reported (Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019), and increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decayed during the locomotion bout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) consistent with earlier work (Reimer et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Within a field of view, individual LC axon segments exhibit highly correlated activity.
claims.source: We found that within a FoV, individual axon segments exhibited highly correlated activity (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claims.claim: LC axons show significant increases in fluorescence following mismatch presentations.
claims.source: Indeed, LC axons showed significant increases in fluorescence following mismatch presentations (Figure 1C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–D.

claims.claim: Responses of LC axons to playback halts when the mouse was stationary were negative and substantially different from mismatch responses.
claims.source: Responses of LC axons to playback halts when the mouse was stationary were negative and substantially different from mismatch responses (Figure 1C–D), demonstrating that the response of LC axons to visuomotor mismatch cannot be explained by the visual stimulus alone.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–D.

claims.claim: The response of LC axons to visuomotor mismatch cannot be explained by the visual stimulus alone.
claims.source: Responses of LC axons to playback halts when the mouse was stationary were negative and substantially different from mismatch responses (Figure 1C–D), demonstrating that the response of LC axons to visuomotor mismatch cannot be explained by the visual stimulus alone.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing mismatch and playback halt responses.

claims.claim: Mismatch responses were significantly larger than playback halt responses that occurred during locomotion in the open loop condition.
claims.source: This indicated that responses in LC axons were acutely dependent on visuomotor coupling, since the only difference between a mismatch stimulus and a playback halt during locomotion is that the former occurs during visuomotor coupling and the latter does not.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing responses under different conditions.

claims.claim: Responses in LC axons are acutely dependent on visuomotor coupling.
claims.source: This indicated that responses in LC axons were acutely dependent on visuomotor coupling, since the only difference between a mismatch stimulus and a playback halt during locomotion is that the former occurs during visuomotor coupling and the latter does not.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing mismatch and playback halt responses during locomotion.

claims.claim: LC axonal mismatch responses increase monotonically with the locomotion speed of the mouse.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that LC axonal mismatch responses increased monotonically with the locomotion speed of the mouse (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: LC axonal responses to visuomotor mismatch are consistent with a visuomotor prediction error signal.
claims.source: Thus, LC axonal responses to visuomotor mismatch are consistent with a visuomotor prediction error signal.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing speed-dependent responses.

claims.claim: LC axons show significant responses to visual flow onsets, but only when the mouse is stationary.
claims.source: We found that LC axons showed significant responses to visual flow onsets, but only when the mouse was stationary (Figure 1F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F–G.

claims.claim: Visual flow onsets during locomotion did not evoke significant responses on average in LC axons.
claims.source: Visual flow onsets during locomotion did not evoke significant responses on average.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on LC axonal responses.

claims.claim: LC axonal responsiveness to visual and visuomotor stimuli is best explained by the absolute error between locomotion and visual flow speeds.
claims.source: Altogether, LC axonal responsiveness to visual and visuomotor stimuli was best explained by the absolute (i.e. unsigned) error between locomotion and visual flow speeds (|Error|=|Speedlocomotion– Speedvisual flow|).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data across multiple stimulus conditions.

claims.claim: LC axonal responses scale with the size of the change in unsigned error magnitude across different stimulus conditions.
claims.source: Changes in the absolute error resulted in corresponding changes in the activity in LC axons (Figure 1C and F), and responses scaled with the size of Δ|Error| (i.e. the change in unsigned error magnitude, see Methods) across the different stimulus conditions (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, F, and H.

claims.claim: Individual LC neurons can preferentially target different cortical areas.
claims.source: Individual LC neurons can preferentially target different cortical areas (Chandler et al., 2019; Kebschull et al., 2016), but it is unclear whether these projection-specific neurons have differing response profiles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical work.

claims.claim: LC axons in anterior and posterior cortex show very similar responses to visuomotor mismatches, playback halts, visual flow onsets, air puffs, and locomotion onsets.
claims.source: We found very similar responses to visuomotor mismatches, playback halts (stationary) and visual flow onsets (stationary; Figure 2B–C), as well as air puffs and locomotion onsets at these two locations (Figure 2B and D), and there were no significant differences in the responses between the two locations.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claims.claim: The LC sends similar visuomotor and locomotion related signals to distinct regions of the cortex.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the idea that the LC sends similar visuomotor and locomotion related signals to distinct regions of the cortex, in line with recent findings showing that LC axons in different cortical regions show responses to the same sensory stimuli (Deitcher et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ChrimsonR resulted in dilations of the right pupil in mice expressing ChrimsonR in a manner that depended on the degree of axon labelling.
claims.source: Optogenetic stimulation, when presented in isolation, resulted in dilations of the right pupil in mice expressing ChrimsonR in a manner that depended on the degree of axon labelling (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but not in control mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Pupil dilation from optogenetic stimulation likely resulted from antidromic activation of the LC.
claims.source: This likely resulted from antidromic activation of the LC, direct stimulation of which is known to produce strong ipsilateral pupil dilation (Liu et al., 2017), and increased our confidence that we were indeed driving LC axons with the parameters selected.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Onset of optogenetic stimulation caused a small calcium response across the population in ChrimsonR-expressing mice that was indistinguishable from that in control mice.
claims.source: Onset of the optogenetic stimulation laser caused a small calcium response across the population in ChrimsonR-expressing mice, which was indistinguishable from that caused in control mice (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The small calcium response to optogenetic stimulation was likely due to a visual effect of the stimulation laser.
claims.source: This was likely due to a visual effect of the stimulation laser.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of responses in ChrimsonR and control mice.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LC axons did not have a direct measurable effect on calcium activity of layer 2/3 neurons in V1.
claims.source: The lack of a difference in this stimulation response between ChrimsonR-expressing mice and control mice indicated that optogenetic stimulation of LC axons did not have a direct measurable effect on calcium activity of L2/3 neurons in V1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing ChrimsonR and control mice.

claims.claim: Responses to visual flow onsets appeared transiently more pronounced during laser stimulation in ChrimsonR-expressing mice only.
claims.source: Responses to visual flow onsets (i.e. at the beginning of the visual flow stimulus, or at the offset of mismatch) appeared transiently more pronounced during laser stimulation in ChrimsonR-expressing mice only (Figure 3E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claims.claim: Averaging across the full response duration, there were no significant effects of laser stimulation on mismatch and visual flow responses.
claims.source: However, this effect was small and not evident in average responses. Averaging across the full response duration, we found no significant effects of laser stimulation, both when comparing trials with and without laser stimulation in the ChrimsonR-expressing group, and when comparing the difference in response size between ChrimsonR-expressing and control mice (Figure 3E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claims.claim: There was no evidence for an effect of optogenetic stimulation of LC axons on average mismatch and visual flow responses across any functional cell groups.
claims.source: We found no evidence for an effect of optogenetic stimulation of LC axons on average mismatch and visual flow responses across any of these cell groups (Figure 3G–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claims.claim: Transient LC axon stimulation in the awake state has only a minor direct effect on the responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1.
claims.source: We thus concluded that transient LC axon stimulation in the awake state has only a minor direct effect on the responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data on optogenetic stimulation effects.

claims.claim: The results are largely in line with recent work demonstrating a lack of effect of LC stimulation on baseline firing in cortical pyramidal neurons, and an enhancement of transient responses to afferent input.
claims.source: These results are largely in line with recent work demonstrating a lack of effect of LC stimulation on baseline firing in cortical pyramidal neurons, and an enhancement of transient responses to afferent input (Vazey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The LC is thought to be involved in cortical plasticity.
claims.source: The LC is thought to be involved in cortical plasticity (Kasamatsu et al., 1985; Kasamatsu and Pettigrew, 1976; Martins and Froemke, 2015; Shepard et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Catecholamine receptors in V1 modulate synaptic plasticity by activating intracellular signaling cascades and interacting with eligibility traces.
claims.source: Catecholamine receptors in V1 are known to modulate synaptic plasticity by activating intracellular signaling cascades and interacting with eligibility traces (Choi et al., 2005; He et al., 2015; Nomura et al., 2014; Seol et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Primary sensory cortices can learn to suppress the sensory consequences of locomotion, driving selective reductions of responses to locomotion-coupled inputs.
claims.source: Primary sensory cortices can indeed learn to suppress the sensory consequences of locomotion, driving selective reductions of responses to locomotion-coupled inputs (Schneider et al., 2018; Widmer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In V1, there is a known increase in the size of visual responses during locomotion compared to stationary periods.
claims.source: In V1, there is a known increase in the size of visual responses during locomotion compared to stationary periods (Bennett et al., 2013; Erisken et al., 2014; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Pakan et al., 2016; Polack et al., 2013; Zmarz and Keller, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The canonical gain increase of visual responses during locomotion was present for control mice but reversed in sign in ChrimsonR-expressing mice.
claims.source: Analyzing only trials where the optogenetic stimulation laser was not on, we found that this canonical gain increase was present for control mice but reversed in sign in ChrimsonR-expressing mice: Visual responses during locomotion were suppressed on average relative to stationary periods (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: ChrimsonR-expressing mice had a significantly lower locomotion modulation index compared to control mice.
claims.source: This resulted in a significantly lower locomotion modulation index (see Methods) for ChrimsonR-expressing relative to control mice (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: The reversal of locomotion modulation index may reflect a result of plasticity induced by earlier LC axon stimulation.
claims.source: Since episodic LC axon stimulation occurred throughout the whole imaging session (i.e. across 10 min in the closed loop condition, prior to the presentation of open loop visual flow stimuli), it is possible that the reversal of locomotion modulation index reflects a result of plasticity induced by earlier LC axon stimulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental design and results.

claims.claim: LC axon stimulation during closed loop visuomotor experience results in a significant reduction in the locomotion modulation index for nasotemporal visual flow responses.
claims.source: Quantifying visual flow responses in high ChrimsonR-expressing mice after optogenetic stimulation during closed loop visuomotor experience revealed a significant reduction in the locomotion modulation index for nasotemporal visual flow responses (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The reduction in locomotion modulation index originated from a reduction in the response to visual flow during locomotion, while responses during stationary periods remained stable.
claims.source: This originated from a reduction in the response to visual flow during locomotion, while responses during stationary periods remained stable (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The effect of LC stimulation on locomotion modulation index was specific to the direction of visual flow seen during forward locomotion.
claims.source: This effect was specific to the direction of visual flow seen during forward locomotion, since locomotion modulation index was preserved for temporonasal visual flow responses (Figure 4D), with negligible changes in response size both during locomotion and stationary periods (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and H.

claims.claim: The effect of LC stimulation on locomotion modulation index was specific to high ChrimsonR-expressing mice.
claims.source: The effect was also specific to high ChrimsonR-expressing mice, as locomotion modulation index did not significantly change in both control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and low ChrimsonR-expressing mice (Figure 4E and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Figure 4E, and Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Stimulating LC axons during open loop replays drove a nonsignificant increase in locomotion modulation index for both nasotemporal and temporonasal visual flow responses.
claims.source: Instead of a stimulus selective reduction in locomotion gain, this paradigm drove a nonsignificant increase in locomotion modulation index for both nasotemporal (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and temporonasal visual flow (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The reduction in locomotion modulation index after stimulation of LC axons in the closed loop condition depends on visuomotor coupling experience.
claims.source: This confirmed that the reduction in locomotion modulation index after stimulation of LC axons in the closed loop condition (Figure 4C) depends on visuomotor coupling experience and is not simply due to exposure to nasotemporal visual flow.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing closed loop and open loop stimulation conditions.

claims.claim: LC axon stimulation over the course of minutes increases locomotion driven suppression of visual flow responses in layer 2/3 in a manner that is specific to reafferent stimulus properties and dependent on both ChrimsonR expression and visuomotor coupling.
claims.source: We conclude that LC axon stimulation over the course of minutes increases locomotion driven suppression of visual flow responses in layer 2/3 in a manner that is specific to reafferent stimulus properties and dependent on both ChrimsonR expression and visuomotor coupling (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data across multiple conditions shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: The effect of LC stimulation on locomotion modulation could not be explained by differences in locomotion behavior between any of the groups analyzed.
claims.source: Importantly, the effect could not be explained by differences in locomotion behavior between any of the groups analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Visual flow responses were amplified during locomotion relative to stationary periods in normally reared mice but were suppressed during locomotion in coupled trained mice.
claims.source: Analyzing responses to nasotemporal visual flow onsets during open loop replay, we found that visual flow responses were amplified during locomotion relative to stationary periods in normally reared mice but were suppressed during locomotion in coupled trained mice (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Coupled trained mice showed a significantly lower locomotion modulation index compared to normally reared mice.
claims.source: This resulted in a significantly lower locomotion modulation index in coupled trained mice compared to normally reared mice (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The effect of coupled training on locomotion modulation index was not due to dark rearing.
claims.source: The effect was not due to dark rearing, as non-coupled trained mice (also dark reared, but with only open loop virtual reality experience Figure 5A; Attinger et al., 2017) showed a positive locomotion modulation index on average that did not significantly differ from that of normally reared mice (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claims.claim: As locomotion speed increased, visual flow responses were increasingly suppressed in coupled trained mice.
claims.source: As locomotion speed increased, visual flow responses were increasingly suppressed in coupled trained mice (Figure 5D), while this was not evident in normally reared mice (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claims.claim: After stimulation of LC axons in closed loop conditions, locomotion modulation index became increasingly negative as locomotion speed increased for nasotemporal visual flow responses in ChrimsonR-expressing mice.
claims.source: For nasotemporal visual flow responses in ChrimsonR-expressing mice, locomotion modulation index was positive and did not change with locomotion speed at the start of the imaging session, but after stimulation of LC axons in closed loop conditions, locomotion modulation index became increasingly negative as locomotion speed increased (Figure 5F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F–G.

claims.claim: The locomotion driven suppression of visual flow emerging after stimulating LC axons in closed loop conditions was locomotion speed dependent in a similar manner to the locomotion driven suppression seen in coupled trained mice.
claims.source: Thus, the locomotion driven suppression of visual flow emerging after stimulating LC axons in closed loop conditions was locomotion speed dependent in a similar manner to the locomotion driven suppression seen in coupled trained mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the speed dependence of suppression in the two groups.

claims.claim: The pattern of differences in locomotion modulation was remarkably similar for ChrimsonR-expressing and coupled trained mice.
claims.source: Overall, the pattern of differences in locomotion modulation was remarkably similar for ChrimsonR-expressing (Figure 5G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and coupled trained mice (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing experimental data across the two groups.

claims.claim: The functional consequence of plasticity evoked by minutes of LC axon stimulation during visuomotor coupling is similar to that seen after experience is developmentally constrained to visuomotor coupling for days.
claims.source: This indicates that the functional consequence of plasticity evoked by minutes of LC axon stimulation during visuomotor coupling is similar to that seen after experience is developmentally constrained to visuomotor coupling for days.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the two experimental paradigms.

claims.claim: The LC responds to unexpected stimuli of various modality, including reward prediction errors, punishment prediction errors, and novel or intense unexpected sensory stimuli.
claims.source: The LC responds to unexpected stimuli of various modality, including reward prediction errors, punishment prediction errors, and novel or intense unexpected sensory stimuli (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Basu et al., 2022; Bouret and Sara, 2004; Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019; Foote et al., 1980; Hervé-Minvielle and Sara, 1995; Su and Cohen, 2022; Takeuchi et al., 2016; Vankov et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The responses found in LC axons to various visual flow stimuli were proportional to the change in the degree of error between visual flow and locomotion speeds.
claims.source: The responses we found in LC axons to the various visual flow stimuli were proportional to the change in the degree of error between visual flow and locomotion speeds (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Prediction errors of all modalities are a general feature of LC signaling.
claims.source: This supports a model in which the LC signals prediction errors, and combined with previous findings, suggests that prediction errors of all modalities are a general feature of LC signaling.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from current and previous findings.

claims.claim: Both positive and negative visuomotor prediction errors appear to be computed in layer 2/3 of the primary visual cortex.
claims.source: Both positive and negative visuomotor prediction errors appear to be computed in layer 2/3 of the primary visual cortex (Jordan and Keller, 2020) and activate the anterior cingulate cortex (Heindorf and Keller, 2022) – an area that projects directly to the LC.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The anterior cingulate cortex is activated by visuomotor prediction errors and projects directly to the LC.
claims.source: Both positive and negative visuomotor prediction errors appear to be computed in layer 2/3 of the primary visual cortex (Jordan and Keller, 2020) and activate the anterior cingulate cortex (Heindorf and Keller, 2022) – an area that projects directly to the LC.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The LC likely inherits prediction errors computed upstream in areas like the cortex.
claims.source: Thus, the LC likely inherits prediction errors computed upstream in areas like the cortex.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from anatomical connectivity and functional data.

claims.claim: The LC integrates prediction errors of all modalities to compute a measure of how inaccurately internal models are currently predicting the global sensory inputs of the animal.
claims.source: Based on the multimodality and unsigned nature of LC responses, and the integrate and broadcast nature of its input-output anatomy (Schwarz et al., 2015), our working model of LC function is as follows: The LC integrates prediction errors of all modalities to compute a measure of how inaccurately internal models are currently predicting the global sensory inputs of the animal.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data and anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: The LC does not signal what type of prediction error occurred, but what the global rate of prediction errors currently is.
claims.source: The LC does not signal what type of prediction error occurred, but what the global rate of prediction errors currently is (i.e. a measure of surprise).
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: The resulting LC output does not directly drive model updating in cortical output areas, but it modulates the rate at which local cortical prediction errors drive plasticity in internal models.
claims.source: The resulting LC output does not directly drive model updating in cortical output areas, but it modulates the rate at which local cortical prediction errors drive plasticity in internal models.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: The specificity of how internal models are changed depends on ongoing prediction errors in the cortex, and the LC input acts to control the learning rate.
claims.source: Thus, the specificity of how internal models are changed depends on ongoing prediction errors in the cortex, and the LC input acts to control the learning rate, modulating the extent to which these cortical prediction errors drive plasticity.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: When prediction error rates are high, updating of internal models will be more rapid as a result of increased LC output.
claims.source: This would allow the LC to be a controller of plasticity in internal models: when prediction error rates are high (i.e. during developmental, novel, or volatile situations), updating of internal models will be more rapid as a result of increased LC output.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: LC calcium responses to locomotion onsets were generally larger than visual flow or visuomotor mismatch responses.
claims.source: LC calcium responses to locomotion onsets, which have been shown previously in LC axons (Deitcher et al., 2019; Reimer et al., 2016), were generally larger than visual flow or visuomotor mismatch responses (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Visuomotor prediction errors contribute to locomotion onset responses in LC axons.
claims.source: We do find that visuomotor prediction errors contribute to locomotion onset responses, as locomotion onset responses in the open loop condition are smaller during visual flow, when locomotion evoked visuomotor error is lower (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: LC calcium activity rises prior to locomotion onset.
claims.source: However, LC calcium activity also rises prior to locomotion onset, creating the additional possibility of an internally generated movement onset response.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on LC activity time courses.

claims.claim: Depleting noradrenaline has been shown to prevent forms of sensory-guided developmental plasticity in the cortex, including ocular dominance plasticity in V1.
claims.source: Depleting noradrenaline has been shown to prevent forms of sensory-guided developmental plasticity in the cortex, including ocular dominance plasticity in V1 (Kasamatsu and Pettigrew, 1976) and changes in the tonotopic map in the auditory cortex (Shepard et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Depleting noradrenaline prevents changes in the tonotopic map in the auditory cortex.
claims.source: Depleting noradrenaline has been shown to prevent forms of sensory-guided developmental plasticity in the cortex, including ocular dominance plasticity in V1 (Kasamatsu and Pettigrew, 1976) and changes in the tonotopic map in the auditory cortex (Shepard et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Acute noradrenergic receptor block can silence neurons in layer 2/3 and massively reduce the amplitude of visual inputs.
claims.source: Indeed, acute noradrenergic receptor block can silence neurons in layer 2/3, and massively reduce the amplitude of visual inputs (Polack et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Electrical stimulation of the LC has been shown to partially restore ocular dominance plasticity in adult cats.
claims.source: In gain-of-function experiments, electrical stimulation of the LC has been shown to partially restore ocular dominance plasticity in adult cats (Kasamatsu et al., 1985).

claims.claim: A few minutes of optogenetic LC axon stimulation in V1 of adult mice during visuomotor coupling can recapitulate the developmental effects of constrained exposure to visuomotor coupling in the virtual reality.
claims.source: Here, we also performed a gain of function experiment: we show that a few minutes of optogenetic LC axon stimulation in V1 of adult mice during visuomotor coupling can recapitulate the developmental effects of constrained exposure to visuomotor coupling in the virtual reality (Figures 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation likely antidromically activates the LC owing to the resulting pupil dilation.
claims.source: We know that we are likely antidromically activating the LC with our optogenetic stimulation owing to the resulting pupil dilation (Figures 3C and 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 4B.

claims.claim: LC neurons are electrically coupled.
claims.source: Given that LC neurons are electrically coupled (McKinney et al., 2022) and have widely divergent axons, our stimulation likely has effects on other LC output targets, such as other neuromodulatory systems, and other areas of the cortex.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.source: Thus, the plasticity effect that we measure may not entirely result from LC output in V1 alone.

claims.claim: The functional impact of LC axon stimulation is strongly suggestive of a role in facilitating plasticity.
claims.source: However, since the LC will never be acting in isolation and broadcasts its output to different cortical areas, the functional impact of LC axon stimulation in this experiment is strongly suggestive of a role in facilitating plasticity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: The plasticity occurs despite only minor effects of LC stimulation on neuronal activity.
claims.source: The fact that the plasticity occurs despite only minor effects of LC stimulation on neuronal activity (Figure 3) indicates that the LC can either enhance plasticity without affecting activity levels, for instance via the molecular cascades or eligibility traces activated by GPCRs (He et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2022; Seol et al., 2007), and/or that a part of the relevant circuit outside of layer 2/3 is more strongly modulated by LC activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3 and citations to previous work.

results.result: LC axons in the cortex respond to unsigned visuomotor prediction errors. LC axonal calcium responses increase with visuomotor mismatches in a speed-dependent manner, respond to unexpected visual flow onsets during stationary periods, and scale with the magnitude of the absolute error between locomotion and visual flow speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C48 provide converging experimental evidence from two-photon calcium imaging showing LC responses to multiple stimulus conditions (mismatches, playback halts, visual flow onsets) with appropriate controls. The speed-dependence (C43), coupling-dependence (C42), and scaling with error magnitude (C48) provide strong support for the prediction error interpretation. Statistical comparisons between conditions are reported with appropriate controls for visual and locomotor confounds.

results.result: LC axons broadcast similar visuomotor prediction error signals across distinct cortical regions. Responses to visuomotor mismatches, visual flow, air puffs, and locomotion onsets were statistically indistinguishable between anterior (motor) and posterior (visual) cortical areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by direct experimental comparison between two imaging window locations (Figure 2B-D) showing no significant differences in LC axonal responses across multiple stimulus types. This supports the broadcast hypothesis, though the sample is limited to two cortical regions and the number of anterior sites (n=9 FoVs) is smaller than posterior (n=31 FoVs).

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of LC axons has minimal direct effects on average calcium responses of layer 2/3 neurons in V1. While transient enhancement of visual flow onset responses was observed, averaging across full response duration showed no significant effects of LC stimulation on mismatch or visual flow responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 are well-supported by experimental data comparing ChrimsonR-expressing and control mice (Figure 3D-H). The use of control mice without LC ChrimsonR expression effectively controls for visual effects of the laser. The lack of effect is consistent across different functional cell types (C59), strengthening the conclusion. However, the negative result depends on the sensitivity of calcium imaging to detect LC-mediated changes.

results.result: ChrimsonR-expressing mice showed reversed locomotion modulation of visual responses compared to controls, with visual responses suppressed rather than enhanced during locomotion. This reversal may reflect plasticity induced by earlier LC axon stimulation during the imaging session.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by experimental data (Figure 3I) showing significant differences between ChrimsonR and control groups. However, C68 is speculative about the mechanism (plasticity vs. other effects). The interpretation that this reflects cumulative plasticity from earlier stimulation is plausible but not directly tested - an alternative explanation could be tonic effects of repeated LC activation.

results.result: Optogenetic LC axon stimulation during closed-loop visuomotor coupling facilitates stimulus-specific suppression of visual responses during locomotion. This effect is specific to nasotemporal visual flow (the reafferent direction), depends on high ChrimsonR expression levels, and requires visuomotor coupling rather than mere visual flow exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C76 provide strong converging evidence for LC-gated plasticity with multiple critical controls: direction specificity (C71), expression-level dependence (C72), coupling requirement (C73-C74), and behavioral controls (C76). The experimental design systematically tests alternative explanations. The comparison between closed-loop and open-loop stimulation (C73-C74) is particularly important for establishing that visuomotor coupling is necessary. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

results.result: LC-induced plasticity over minutes recapitulates the effects of visuomotor learning that normally occur over days of developmental training. Both LC stimulation and coupled training produce locomotion-speed-dependent suppression of visual flow responses with similar patterns across functional cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C84 are supported by comparison between newly acquired data (LC stimulation) and previously published developmental training data. The similarity in locomotion-speed dependence (C80-C82) and patterns across cell types (C83) strengthens the parallel. However, C79's control for dark rearing uses a different dataset (non-coupled trained mice), and the comparison involves different experimental protocols and potentially different analysis methods across datasets, which could introduce confounds.

results.result: Validation of LC axon labeling and recording quality. GCaMP6s-expressing cells in the LC are tyrosine hydroxylase positive, and LC axonal fluorescence shows expected correlations with pupil diameter, responses to air puffs, and locomotion onset dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 provide important validation controls supported by immunohistochemistry (C33) and comparison with previous literature (C34-C36). The high correlation between axon segments within a field of view (C37) is documented but creates an analytical challenge that the authors address by pooling data within FoVs.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation produces pupil dilation in ChrimsonR-expressing mice in a manner dependent on axon labeling density, likely due to antidromic activation of the LC.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 and C104 are supported by experimental data (Figures 3C, 4B) showing expression-dependent pupil dilation. The inference of antidromic activation (C53, C104) is reasonable given the known effects of LC stimulation on pupil diameter, though direct confirmation of antidromic activation is not provided.

results.result: Proposed working model: The LC integrates prediction errors across modalities to compute a global measure of prediction inaccuracy, broadcasting this signal to modulate cortical learning rates rather than directly driving plasticity. This allows adaptive control of internal model updating based on environmental volatility.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 present a theoretical model that is consistent with the experimental findings but goes beyond what is directly demonstrated. The model makes specific claims about LC computation (integration across modalities, unsigned nature) and function (learning rate modulation) that are plausible interpretations but remain speculative. The data support that LC responds to prediction errors and facilitates plasticity, but do not directly test the integration, broadcasting, or learning rate modulation mechanisms proposed.

results.result: LC responses to locomotion onsets are larger than visuomotor mismatch responses and may reflect multiple sources including visuomotor prediction errors and internally generated movement signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by experimental data showing larger locomotion onset responses and their partial dependence on visuomotor coupling (C97). The acknowledgment of multiple potential sources (C98) is appropriately cautious. However, the interpretation remains somewhat uncertain as the relative contributions of different error types cannot be fully disentangled.

results.result: The measured plasticity effects may not result entirely from LC output in V1 alone, as LC neurons are electrically coupled and have divergent projections. However, the functional impact strongly suggests a role in facilitating plasticity, potentially through molecular cascades or modulation of circuits outside layer 2/3.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 provide important caveats about interpretation. C105 is supported by citation, and C106-C107 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the optogenetic approach. C108 offers plausible mechanistic explanations for how plasticity occurs despite minimal activity effects, supported by citations to GPCR signaling literature. This represents good scientific practice in acknowledging limitations.

results.result: Proposed general principle: Catecholamines gate plasticity underlying predictive learning across all modalities, extending beyond reward learning to sensorimotor associations.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 proposes a broad generalization based on the current visuomotor findings and previous reward learning literature. While the parallel is conceptually appealing and the current data support the principle in the visuomotor domain, the claim of generality across "all modalities" exceeds what is directly demonstrated. This represents a hypothesis for future testing rather than a supported conclusion.

results.result: LC axons in the cortex respond to visuomotor mismatches in a manner consistent with unsigned prediction error signaling. The responses scale with locomotion speed, are dependent on visuomotor coupling, and cannot be explained by visual stimuli alone.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the study provides 'convincing evidence that locus coeruleus is activated during visuomotor mismatches.' Reviewer 2 notes 'LC axons responded selectively to a mismatch between the visual input and locomotion' with 'the greater the mismatch...the larger the LC response.' Reviewer 3 describes 'calcium responses proportional to absolute prediction errors.' No concerns are raised about these core observations.

results.result: LC response profiles are similar in both motor and visual cortical areas, indicating that LC axons broadcast prediction error signals throughout the dorsal cortex.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'This seemed to be a global response as LC responses were indistinguishable between sensory and motor cortical areas.' Reviewer 3 notes the signals were 'non-specifically broadcast across the dorsal cortex.' The broadcast nature of LC signaling is treated as an established result.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of LC axons during closed-loop visuomotor experience facilitates learning of stimulus-specific suppression of visual responses during locomotion. This plasticity is specific to reafferent stimulus properties, depends on ChrimsonR expression level, and requires visuomotor coupling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this plasticity result. Reviewer 1 states 'Gain of function optogenetic experiments complement this evidence and indicate that locus coeruleus could be involved in the learning process.' Reviewer 2 notes 'LC drove learning (updating the internal model)' and 'Responses in the visual cortex increased with locomotion, and this was suppressed following LC phasic stimulation during visuomotor coupled training.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'changes in the effect of locomotion on visually evoked activity after repeated LC axons activation' with appropriate controls.

results.result: LC-induced plasticity over minutes recapitulates the effect of visuomotor learning that normally occurs during developmental visuomotor coupling over days. The speed-dependent locomotion modulation patterns are remarkably similar between optogenetically-stimulated mice and coupled-trained mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this comparison as valid. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'artificial optogenetic stimulation of LC permitted plasticity over minutes, which would normally take days in non-stimulated mice trained in the visuomotor coupling mode.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Based on similar locomotion modulation index dependency on speed observed in mice that develop only with visuomotor experience...the authors concluded that changes in locomotion modulation index are the result of experience-dependent plasticity occurring at a much faster rate during LC axons optogenetic stimulations.' No concerns are raised about this key comparison.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of LC axons has minimal direct acute effects on calcium activity of layer 2/3 neurons in V1, with only transient enhancement of visual flow onset responses but no significant effects on average mismatch and visual flow responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding without challenge. Reviewer 2 states 'LC optical stimulation failed to alter acute cellular responses' and 'LC drove learning (updating the internal model) despite that LC optical stimulation failed to alter acute cellular responses.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Although LC activation had little impact on evoked activity related to visuomotor prediction errors, the authors observed changes in the effect of locomotion.' This dissociation between acute effects and plasticity is accepted as a key finding.

results.result: Prediction errors drive LC activity, and combined with previous findings on reward and action prediction errors, this suggests that prediction errors of all modalities are a general feature of LC signaling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support this interpretive claim. Reviewer 2 states the data 'support the framework that LC acts as a prediction error detector.' Reviewer 1 notes the study 'provides convincing evidence that locus coeruleus is activated during visuomotor mismatches' and 'sets the groundwork for the circuit dissection of predictive signals.' The generalization to multimodal prediction errors is implicitly accepted through the reviewers' positive framing of the LC as a prediction error detector.

results.result: Validation of LC axon labeling and characterization: GCaMP6s-positive cells are tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactive, axonal fluorescence correlates with pupil diameter, LC axons respond to air puffs, show locomotion onset responses, and exhibit highly correlated activity within a field of view.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept these methodological validations by not questioning the identity or properties of the labeled LC axons. Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors carefully designed experiments and corresponding controls to exclude any confounding factors in the interpretation of neuronal activity in LC axons.' The characterization data are treated as establishing the validity of the preparation.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation produces pupil dilation in ChrimsonR-expressing mice in a manner dependent on axon labeling density, likely due to antidromic activation of the LC.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this interpretation. The pupil dilation is used as evidence of effective LC activation. Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'confirmed that this plasticity depended on the density of LC axons activated,' implicitly accepting the pupil dilation as a valid indicator of LC activation level.

results.result: ChrimsonR-expressing mice show reversed locomotion modulation of visual responses compared to controls, with visual responses suppressed during locomotion rather than enhanced. This may reflect plasticity induced by earlier LC axon stimulation during the imaging session.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this observation as evidence of LC-induced plasticity. Reviewer 2 notes 'Responses in the visual cortex increased with locomotion, and this was suppressed following LC phasic stimulation during visuomotor coupled training (closed loop).' The reversal is treated as a key result supporting the plasticity hypothesis, though the speculative nature of the timing interpretation is acknowledged by the authors and not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: The effect of LC stimulation on locomotion modulation cannot be explained by differences in locomotion behavior between experimental groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this control by not raising concerns about behavioral confounds. Reviewer 3 explicitly praises the study: 'The authors carefully designed experiments and corresponding controls to exclude any confounding factors in the interpretation of neuronal activity.' This control is treated as adequately addressing potential confounds.

results.result: The authors propose a working model where the LC integrates multimodal prediction errors to compute a global measure of prediction accuracy, broadcasting this signal to modulate learning rates in cortical circuits without directly driving model updating.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support this interpretive framework. Reviewer 1 states the results 'indicate that locus coeruleus could be involved in the learning process that enables visuomotor predictions.' Reviewer 2 notes the data 'support the framework that LC acts as a prediction error detector and supervises cortical plasticity to update internal representations.' Reviewer 3 states the study will 'have an important contribution to the field of system neuroscience by shedding new light on the role of a key neuromodulator.' The model is treated as well-supported by the data.

results.result: LC calcium responses to locomotion onsets are generally larger than visuomotor mismatch responses. Visuomotor prediction errors contribute to these responses, but LC activity also rises prior to locomotion onset, suggesting an internally generated component.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations about locomotion onset responses. The findings are presented as part of the characterization of LC activity patterns and are implicitly accepted through the lack of critique.

results.result: The plasticity effect may not result entirely from LC output in V1 alone due to electrical coupling of LC neurons and widespread axonal projections, but the functional impact is strongly suggestive of a role in facilitating plasticity despite minimal effects on acute neuronal activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these caveats and interpretations. Reviewer 2 notes 'LC drove learning (updating the internal model) despite that LC optical stimulation failed to alter acute cellular responses,' acknowledging the dissociation. Reviewer 3 states 'The results provide strong support for the claims of the study' despite these acknowledged limitations. The interpretation that LC facilitates plasticity through mechanisms beyond acute activity modulation is treated as reasonable.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on LC activation during visuomotor mismatches (C1, C38-C48). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing, noting speed-dependence, coupling-dependence, and scaling with error magnitude. Both rate as SUPPORTED with no concerns raised.

Strong agreement on broadcast signaling (C2, C50-C51). Both evaluations accept that LC responses are indistinguishable across cortical regions. OpenEval notes sample size limitation (fewer anterior sites), while peer reviewers accept without challenge. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Complete agreement on lack of acute activity effects (C54-C60). Both evaluations accept that LC stimulation does not alter immediate cellular responses despite driving plasticity. Both note this dissociation as a key finding and rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on reversal of locomotion modulation (C66-C68). Both accept the experimental findings showing differences between ChrimsonR and control groups. OpenEval explicitly notes C68's mechanistic interpretation as speculative, while peer reviewers accept without challenging the timing interpretation. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on LC-gated plasticity (C3, C69-C76). Both evaluations praise the experimental design with multiple controls (direction specificity, expression-dependence, coupling requirement). OpenEval emphasizes C73-C74 closed/open-loop comparison; peer reviewers highlight the overall plasticity result. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on comparison with developmental training (C4, C77-C84). Both accept the parallel between optogenetic LC stimulation and natural developmental plasticity. OpenEval raises concern about comparing different datasets and protocols (C79 control); peer reviewers accept without noting this limitation. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on methodological validations (C33-C37). Both evaluations accept the immunohistochemistry and characterization data as establishing validity of the LC axon preparation. Peer reviewers implicitly accept by not questioning; OpenEval explicitly notes these as important validation controls. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on pupil dilation as LC activation indicator (C52-C53, C104). Both accept expression-dependent pupil dilation as evidence of effective LC activation. OpenEval notes the inference of antidromic activation is reasonable but not directly confirmed; peer reviewers accept without challenge. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Divergent evaluations of theoretical model (C91-C95). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the model goes beyond what is directly demonstrated and remains speculative regarding integration, broadcasting, and learning rate modulation mechanisms. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, treating the framework as well-supported and an important contribution. This represents the most significant disagreement.

Agreement on locomotion onset responses (C96-C98). Both evaluations accept the findings about larger responses at locomotion onset and partial coupling-dependence. OpenEval notes appropriate caution about multiple potential sources; peer reviewers accept without detailed comment. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on interpretive caveats (C105-C108). Both evaluations accept the acknowledged limitations regarding optogenetic approach and mechanisms of plasticity without acute activity changes. Both view these caveats as appropriate scientific practice. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Partial overlap on behavioral controls (C76). OpenEval includes C76 in broader plasticity evaluation (R5); peer reviewers evaluate C76 separately as a control for behavioral confounds. Both accept the control as adequate and rate as SUPPORTED.

OpenEval evaluates broad generalization claim (C113) as UNCERTAIN, noting it exceeds what is directly demonstrated and represents a hypothesis for future testing rather than a supported conclusion. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

Peer reviewers evaluate interpretive claim about LC as multimodal prediction error detector (C5, C86-C87) as SUPPORTED, treating the generalization as well-established. OpenEval does not have a separate evaluation for these specific claims, though related theoretical claims are evaluated in R9 as UNCERTAIN.
